So your thinking of getting into butchery. The very first place to start is a good set of knives.

A great knife will last you a lifetime. I still have my grandfather's knives from when he owned a grocery store in the 60s. And they are still sharp! It is an investment, and if you treat it right, it will take care of you. You don't have to go and buy a $500 knife. Victorinox makes great knives for a good price.

I personally own about 25 knives that I use regularly. Each has a purpose, and it is good to understand what each does and how to use them. For home or personal use, 2-3 good knives will work.

I recommend you start off with a 6 in semi-flexible and either a 8 in chef or a 10 in slicer knife, you can add knives from there.

Types of knives

There are thousands of types, so I'm not talking about any of them. You want to match the knife to the job. With only a few knives this does become difficult, so expand your knife set if you find yourself needing a knife multiple times a week. Watch this video for some of the types of knives

Different knife features

  • Granton Edge: This has a little scalloped on either side that creates a air cushion for smoother, cleaner cuts. It doesn't tear or rip the meat your cutting.

  • Flexible and semi-flex: This lets you bend around bones or follow seams. It lets you also fillet things easier. A stiff knife lets you have maximum cutting strength. The flexible will bend and let you smoothly cut around stuff.

*Handles:They usually only come in wood or plastic, though there are specialty ones you can buy. Wood will crack and needs to be replaced sooner than plastic. Wood must be oiled regularly to prevent drying and cracking. Plastic handles are also more hygienic, since they don't absorb stuff like wood.

  • Understand where the steel comes from: A European steel knife is softer will be easier to sharpen, but loses its edge quickly and a Japanese knife is harder will be harder to sharpen, but loses its edge slowly. A ceramic knife is an option, and will hold an edge for a long time, but needs to be professionally sharpened. They are also very brittle. Steel also gets sharper than ceramics. If your not going to put the effort in to take care of your knife, get a ceramic one.

Maintenance and care

  • Day to day maintenance: After each use, carefully hand wash, hand dry, and oil the blade. Only use mineral oil since it is the only one that does not go rancid. Never use a dish washer. It is very bad for the edge, and wooden handled ones will dry and crack faster. The oil and hand drying will prevent damage to the blade.

*Storage: Never store knives in a drawer. They bang against other stuff, and you can cut yourself if you aren't careful. A knife block is an option, but I don't like them because the edge is resting on something. I prefer a magnet or a knife case. The only reason to buy a knife case, if your a chef or meat cutter, and are bringing your knives with you all the time. If you are moving your knifes, aluminum foil or plastic wrap will protect the knives and protect yourself from accidentally cutting yourself.

Sharpening

I was going to put this under maintenance and care, but it is such an important and often asked about item, it gets its own category.

A sharp knife is precise, uses less effort and if you do cut yourself, the cut is way better. A dull knife rips and tears. I cut my thumb almost off with a super sharp thing, it was a lot better than cutting it with a dull one.

There are hundreds of ways to sharpen a knife. They all have one thing in common, time and effort. http://veuwer.com/i/2pis,2pit This is a rough graphic of what happens to a knife after wear and tear. A knife is tiny serrations, and after a while, the serrations get knocked out of line. This can be fixed with a honing rod or a chantry knife sharpener.

After a while the edge wears down and round out, you need to use an oilstone or whetstone. Neither are expensive to buy.

The actual technique, watch this video.

Extra stuff!

  • A cutting glove is a must if your not experienced with a knife, or plan on doing a lot of cutting, BUY ONE. They are worth it. I prefer metal ones rather than Kevlar gloves. The Kevlar will start to smell and gets nasty. Kevlar ones are cheaper, and start at $10. Metal ones start at $100.

  • Cutting through bones: A cleaver or saw will work. Cleavers are imprecise, unless your practiced. A saw is better in all ways, IMHO. Cleavers should never be used for anything bigger than 3 inches. Keep your hands out of the way.

Happy cutting!
